text: Measured 2026-09-21 minutes after initializing this campaign: the managed signal block in AGENTS.md prints "attention: run harden-chain-and-verification-2-verification-fairness needs you - verification_failed" underneath campaign durable-state-integrity. That run belongs to harden-chain-and-verification, closed 2026-09-17, and this campaign was created minutes ago with an empty projection (its projection.json carries no attention at all). The cause is src/repo/signal.mjs:144, which selects an inbox entry when entry.campaignId === campaign.id OR entry.campaignId === null. Every one of the 12 attention entries in runs/inbox.jsonl carries campaignId null, so an orphan attention is attributed to every campaign at once, forever. The attribution is recoverable and is being thrown away: each entry does carry runId, and a run belongs to exactly one campaign. Two candidate fixes, both honest: stamp campaignId at write time from the run the attention is about, or resolve it from runId at read time and show an attention that still cannot be attributed under no campaign rather than under all of them. This matters more than a cosmetic line: AGENTS.md is the first thing any agent reads in this repository, the signal block exists to tell it what to continue, and it is currently naming the wrong campaign. Same theme as R5 and R6 of this campaign - the record layer telling the truth - so it belongs in phase 3 rather than in a campaign of its own. Not folded into the committed SPEC.md on purpose: phase 1 is already running against a spec carved from it, and amending a committed campaign record mid-run is the mutation this repository has a rule against. It goes into the phase 3 spec when that phase is carved.

Measured 2026-09-21 on the first planning run of this campaign, phase cancel-keeps-integrated-work. Review round 1 returned 3 findings with 1 critical and, separately, a freeze preflight refusal: "sizing_single_node_plan: node cancel-preserves-integrated-heads is the plans only node; pass options.targetedFix to allow a single-node plan" (src/plan/sizing.mjs:66). The advice names an option the operator cannot supply. src/plan/sizing.mjs declares targetedFix in SizingOptions, src/plan/pipeline.mjs:246 builds those options with nodeBudgetMs, facts, minWriteFiles and turnCeiling and never passes it, and faberun plan exposes no flag for it. So a phase that legitimately wants one node can never freeze through the CLI. This is the same class as the ratchet advice fixed in 2c9dd69: the engine tells the operator to do something the product gives them no way to do. It is also the same pressure as the scope finding fixed in 2a3c73c, from the other direction: there the message invited the reviser to write less, here the refusal invites it to split one coherent change into two nodes purely to satisfy a count. This phase is the honest example. R1 and R2 are one change to src/engine/cancel.mjs - create a ref per non-null integratedHead before releasing anything, and name what was preserved in the output - and the drafter was right to emit one node for it. Candidate fix, cheapest honest version: a faberun plan flag that sets targetedFix, refused unless the spec really is small, so the operator can say once that a phase is a targeted fix instead of the reviser inventing a second node. Recording rather than acting: the pipeline is mid-flight on revise round 1 and the outcome is evidence either way. If it contests, the draft contract on disk is still reviewable and the phase can be authored from it.

Correction to open-question plan-cannot-freeze-a-legitimately-single-node-phase, written 2026-09-21 after watching revise round 1 finish. That note predicted the sizing refusal would push the reviser to split one coherent change into two nodes purely to satisfy a count. It did not happen on this example, and the prediction was wrong. The reviser produced a layered two-node graph with a real dependency: worktree-preserve-ref-verb writes src/repo/worktree.mjs and creates test/repo/worktree.test.mjs, and cancel-preserves-integrated-heads writes src/engine/cancel.mjs and test/engine/cancel.test.mjs depending on it. That is a defensible decomposition rather than a padded one, and it matches this repository layering, where repo/ owns git and engine/ owns the control loop. Two further checks of the same output, both passing. The reviser claimed a measured 24.7s for the existing test/engine/cancel.test.mjs at 235e383; measuring it here now gives 22s, the same ballpark, so it ran the command instead of inventing the number. And test/repo/worktree.test.mjs genuinely does not exist yet, so listing it is the node creating it, which is what the test-mirrors-src rule asks for. What survives of the original finding is narrower and still real: targetedFix is declared in src/plan/sizing.mjs, is never passed by src/plan/pipeline.mjs:246, and has no flag on faberun plan, so the refusal message names an option the operator cannot supply. That is a dead-end diagnostic and worth fixing. What does not survive is the claim that the refusal degrades plan quality. On the one phase where it has been observed, the plan it forced is better than the one it refused.

Plan for phase cancel-keeps-integrated-work is contested after 2 review round(s): task packet scope does not close; declare in readFiles or writeFiles, or acknowledge in scopeAcknowledged: nodes[0] (worktree-preserve-ref-verb): test/engine/cancel.test.mjs (cross-node: this node writes src/repo/worktree.mjs, which cancel-preserves-integrated-heads wrote a test against; declare test/engine/cancel.test.mjs in writeFiles or scopeAcknowledged so this node may change the test its work breaks) Resolve it by declaring each named file in writeFiles — or acknowledging it in scopeAcknowledged when the node must not change it — never by dropping a write the node needs: removing a file from writeFiles clears this failure too, and leaves the worker without a file the work requires.; Node cancel-preserves-integrated-heads no longer declares src/repo/worktree.mjs in writeFiles, which the plan this revise revised did declare. Declare it again: the resolution to a scope-closure finding is to declare or acknowledge the dragged-along file, never to drop a write the node needs — a smaller write set clears the same finding while leaving the worker unable to do the work.

A DoD command proof that uses node --test --test-name-pattern passes when the pattern matches nothing, and nothing in the output says so. Measured 2026-09-21 against the integrated tree 6e5e752 of this phase: node --test --test-name-pattern="zzz-este-teste-nao-existe" test/engine/cancel.test.mjs prints a tick for the FILE, reports tests 1, pass 1, fail 0 and exits 0 - byte-identical in shape to a pattern that genuinely matches one test. The tick is the file counted as a unit, not a test that ran. Neither the exit code nor the counters distinguish a real pass from a vacuous one. This bit this very phase. Three of the six DoD items I authored named patterns no test carries: "cancel keeps integrated work reachable", "cancel reports what it preserved" and "relaunch after cancel" matched zero tests each, and the gate still reported that every deterministic Definition of Done item passed. The work itself is sound - the worker wrote four real tests, including a genuine relaunch that drives runContract rather than a refusal scan - but the gate that certified it was measuring nothing on half its items. Two distinct defects, and only the second is the products. Mine: a --test-name-pattern proof must name a string the packet REQUIRES the worker to use, or must not use a pattern at all; I copied pattern text out of the plan and never pinned the test names. The products: faberun accepts a proof command that ran zero tests as proof. A gate that cannot fail is decoration, which is this repositorys own phrasing for the rule it applies to itself. Candidate fix, cheapest honest version: when a verification or DoD command carries --test-name-pattern, refuse the result unless the run reports at least one test actually executed. Recording rather than acting: phase 1 is still to be reviewed and promoted, and the fix belongs in its own change. It is the sharpest finding of the day and should not wait long.

Phase 1 (R1, R2) landed on main as d362a10 and 15e1e24, two commits along the repository layer boundary. Both nodes passed on attempt 1 with a deterministic gate; the judge was never invoked because every DoD item is a command proof, so the phase cost USD 0.0948 in worker tokens and nothing in judge tokens. Exactly the four declared files changed, zero unexpected paths. What landed: createPreservedRef and preservedRefName in src/repo/worktree.mjs put refs/faberun/<run-id>/preserved/<node-id> at a node integrated commit, idempotent by the same contract deleteRef honours; cancelRun creates one such ref for every non-null integratedHead before it releases anything, returns the refs preserved alongside the artifacts released instead of a bare true, and its misleading comment is corrected. A node that never integrated gets no ref. Reviewed rather than trusted, and the review found something the gate did not. Three of the six DoD proofs used --test-name-pattern strings no test carried and passed vacuously; see the open-question a-test-name-pattern-that-matches-nothing-passes. So the work was verified here by hand instead: all nine tests read and run green (six in cancel.test.mjs, three in worktree.test.mjs), and the central claim was checked in both directions. The gc test is better than the spec asked for - it asserts the preserved ref is the only ref left and expires reflogs first, with a comment saying a reflog would root the commit and let the test pass for the wrong reason. The other direction was measured in a scratch repository: delete the branch, expire reflogs, git gc --prune=now, and the commit is gone. The relaunch proof is real, driving runContract rather than asserting a refusal scan stays quiet. The authoring lesson landed as a third packet rule in AGENTS.md at 5ca2dbf.

Plan for phase a-suite-run-leaves-no-trace is contested after 3 review round(s): The proposed R4 ratchet only runs a generated canary through test/run-suite.mjs and checks that package.json still names that entry. It does not snapshot and enforce the operator home around the complete child suite. A newly added test can unset or override FABERUN_HOME, or otherwise write to the real resolved home, and npm test can still pass, so the plan does not satisfy the requirement that no new test file can reintroduce the leak by measuring the suite's effect.; plan.nodes[0].definitionOfDone[1].proof.ref must be the zero-based index of a verification command; plan.nodes[0].verification[2].timeoutSec must be between 0 and 600

Phase 2 contested after 3 rounds, and both extra rounds were spent on plan shape rather than substance. The five findings are the three from review round 1, carried forward unresolved, plus two structural refusals: revise attempt 1 emitted proof.ref as a command string where kind verification requires a zero-based index, and revise attempt 2 emitted verification[2].timeoutSec of 2400 where VERIFICATION_LIMITS.maxTimeoutSec is 600. So raising --review-rounds from 2 to 3 changed nothing measurable: the reviser never produced a valid plan for the reviewer to look at twice, and F1, F2 and F3 were never addressed. An invalid plan consuming a review round is worth its own look; the budget is meant for convergence on substance. The second refusal exposes a real collision between the product and my own spec. No declared verification command may exceed 600 seconds. A full npm test on this tree runs about 2100. R3 as I wrote it asks for proof that a complete npm test leaves the operator home untouched, and that proof cannot be expressed as a verification command at all. The reviser was not wrong to want 2400s; it was asking for something the schema forbids. The honest design falls out of taking the cap seriously, and it is better than what the plan proposed. Prove the mechanism where it is cheap and the effect where it already runs: a static ratchet in test/repo/source-shape.test.mjs that no test file unsets or overrides FABERUN_HOME, which is milliseconds and is what R4 actually asks for; a fast test that the scoped home reaches every test process; and the before-and-after snapshot of the real home wrapped around the npm test step that ci.yml line 29 already runs, which has no 600s cap and costs no extra wall clock. Both of my own objections to the draft were wrong, and wrong the same way. I called test/run-suite.mjs unnecessary indirection and I called touching .github/workflows/ci.yml scope creep. The wrapper carries the snapshot the requirement needs, and ci.yml is exactly where the full-suite proof belongs. I prune…

Tail of the previous note, which R5 ate while I was writing about R5. Measured 2026-09-21: 2131 bytes sent, 2048 stored, truncated with an ellipsis, and the CLI answered "[campaign] open-question noted" -- success. The lost sentence was my own self-correction, which is the part a reader would most want. This is the sharpest demonstration of R5 the campaign will get: the note documenting a silent-discard defect was silently discarded, and the tool reported it worked. It also shows the remedy R5 names is the right one. A refusal naming the cap and the size received would have cost me one retry; the silent success cost the content and I only noticed because I had counted the bytes myself beforehand. An author who does not count never learns. The lost text, restored: both of my own objections to the phase 2 draft were wrong, and wrong the same way. I called test/run-suite.mjs unnecessary indirection, and I called touching .github/workflows/ci.yml scope creep. The wrapper is what carries the home snapshot the requirement needs, and ci.yml line 29 is exactly where the full-suite proof belongs, because it already runs npm test and has no 600-second cap. I pruned toward smaller and simpler without checking the constraint that made the larger thing necessary. Twice on one plan, in the same direction.

Node no-test-file-can-reach-the-real-home lost attempt 1 to the machine, not to its own work. The gate reported "deterministic verification failed" with evidence "node --test test/engine/: exit=-, exit=-" -- no exit code, twice, which is a kill by signal rather than a red test. Measured 2026-09-21 at the moment of the failure: swap 8427 MB used of 9216, 91 percent, 7.1 million pageouts, 33 percent system-wide memory free. No single runaway process; the machine carries 19 Claude Code sessions, a 1.2 GB browser and a faberun dashboard with live connections, none of them mine to stop. The mechanism is mine to avoid, though, and I had already written it down and not applied it. node --test <directory> runs its files concurrently, defaulting to the CPU count, so the finalVerification command node --test test/engine/ spawns dozens of node processes at once. Under 91 percent swap that is what gets killed. My own memory note faberun-test-env-gotchas says to use --test-concurrency=1 when a campaign is verifying, and I authored both verification suites of this campaign without it. Two consequences. The node carries maxRevisions 1, so attempt 2 is its last; if the machine kills it again the node parks on revision_cap for an environmental reason and the work is sound. And every heavy verification command in this campaign has the same exposure: test/engine/ at 158 seconds idle, test/repo/ at 35, and the finalVerification group that runs six directories. The fix for the next contract is to declare --test-concurrency=1 on every directory-wide verification command, and to keep measuring duration with that flag on, since serialising changes the number. Not applying it to the running contract: it cannot be changed mid-flight, and cancelling to relaunch would cost more than the one attempt that remains.

Phase 2 (R3, R4) landed on main as e0bab91 and 49f2665. The run did not close it: node 2 exhausted on revision_cap with verification_failed, and the evidence was the same on both attempts -- "node --test test/engine/: exit=-, exit=-", no exit code, which is a kill by signal under memory pressure and not a red test. Swap was at 8427 MB of 9216 when attempt 1 died. The work was sound the whole time; attempt 1 had already committed it as 4ac28ca and attempt 2 found the tree already implemented. Landed by hand after verifying it four ways, because a gate that died environmentally certified nothing. The workflow YAML folds as intended: parsed with js-yaml, the step is exactly "npm test && test ! -e $HOME/.faberun", so the assertion is real and runs in the same step. The static ratchet discriminates: 17 of 17 green at baseline, and injecting a bare delete of process.env.FABERUN_HOME turns it red naming file and line. The two failures seen in a fresh worktree -- commitlint and hooks -- reproduce identically on main in a worktree, so they are the missing node_modules and husky, not a regression; in the real checkout the same suites are 150 pass, 0 fail with typecheck clean. And the effect is closed: test/contract/derived-fields.test.mjs, which wrote a record every single run for three days, now writes none without having been edited, 402 records before and after. Two things the node taught that the packet had wrong. My premise that only test/scoped-home.mjs would own FABERUN_HOME was false: 26 write sites across 19 files already set it, in two legitimate idioms, so the rule had to hold the tree to the effect rather than to one owner. And the CI assertion had to fold into the existing npm test step rather than become a new one, because test/host/ci-policy.test.mjs pins that job step list and the packet forbade editing it.

Found while verifying R9 against the live tree, and it is a separate problem from the one R9 fixes. The managed signal block is byte-bounded, and the bound is being spent on parked runs of campaigns that are already closed. Measured 2026-09-21 rendering the block against this operator runs directory: 20 lines, 2932 bytes, ending in the truncation marker. Eight of those lines are parked runs from adversarial-planner, become-faberun, chain-ergonomics-and-fairness and env-independence-and-generated-docs, all closed campaigns whose parked runs the owner has already decided are historical record rather than backlog (roadmap decision D1). The consequence is concrete. R9 makes an unattributable attention appear once at run level instead of under every campaign, and its own test proves the line is produced and visible. In the live tree that line is truncated away, so the operator sees nothing at all. R9 is satisfied -- the wrong attribution is gone and the line exists -- but the visibility R9 promises is consumed by lines describing work nobody intends to resume. This is not the node failing. It is my own scoping showing its cost: the packet said not to change the byte budget or the truncation of the block, so the node could not have addressed it. Candidate fix, and it is a decision rather than a defect: a parked run of a closed campaign is record, not signal, and the block could omit it or rank it below anything from an active campaign. The block is the first thing every agent reads in this repository, and today most of its budget describes campaigns nobody is working on. Worth raising with whoever owns the roadmap, since D1 already decided those runs are not backlog.

Phase 3 (R5, R8, R9) landed on main as 5903777, afb4cd7 and 3b15947. Three nodes, three passes on the first attempt, gates all deterministic so the judge was never invoked: USD 0.188 in worker tokens and nothing in judge tokens. Exactly the seven declared files changed, 459 insertions, zero unexpected paths. The verification design held where phase 2 died. Every directory-wide command carried --test-concurrency=1 with a timeout measured under that flag, and test/engine/ was left out of the arrays entirely because it cannot be measured on this machine right now -- the attempt to measure it was killed for low memory. Nothing was killed this time. Verified by hand on the landed tree: 186 passes across test/campaign/ and test/repo/, 15 across the touched engine files, typecheck clean. What the nodes taught that the packets had wrong. The R8 node found two node --test traps I did not know and my packet got one of them backwards: a --test-reporter after a test file is ignored because node reads its own options left to right, so my instruction to append it would have been a silent no-op; and a nested node --test inheriting NODE_TEST_CONTEXT emits no TAP at all. Either alone would have made the empty-filter refusal a gate that never fires, which is the defect it exists to remove. Both are now in AGENTS.md at ff72121. The R5 node improved on the requirement: the refusal names the size, the cap and how many bytes to cut, which is what an author actually needs, and it drew a line worth keeping -- truncating a display is honest, truncating a record is not, so boundedText keeps its 44 rendering callers. The R9 node resolves attribution from the campaigns own linkedRunIds rather than from any guess.

Node the-migration-completes-or-says-what-blocks-it died at 2m19s on its first attempt with code incomplete_stream and the message "ZCode emitted no result object: ... Error: Turn was cancelled. (traceId: 0a53ddb6)". The provider turn was cancelled upstream; the node had produced nothing. Two things worth separating. First, incomplete_stream is not in AUTO_RETRY_CODES, which today holds judge_unavailable, provider_error, stall_timeout, wall_clock_timeout and turn_limit. A stream that ends with no result object because the provider turn was cancelled is as transient as a provider_error, the node did no work, and the automatic retry is already capped at one by autoRetryConsumed. The argument against is that an incomplete_stream caused by a systematic protocol mismatch would retry and fail identically, burning the attempt -- but that argument applies equally to provider_error, which does retry. Candidate: add incomplete_stream to the set, or split the code so a cancelled turn is distinguishable from a malformed stream. Second, and closer to this campaign theme: the node terminal state is canceled. That is the same word the product uses when the operator cancels a run, and here nobody cancelled anything -- the provider did. An operator reading status sees canceled and reasonably concludes a human stopped it. The state should say what happened. Recording rather than acting: the run is resumable and the node did no work, so the cost of the event was two minutes. Neither change belongs in this phase, whose contract is already authored and whose other node landed clean.

R7 is half satisfied, and acting on the fix exposed the other half. The verification refusal now carries its resolution, and I followed it: copied .runs/control/second-opinions into the published copy by hand, as the message instructed, and migrate advanced past verification for the first time in days. It then failed at the removal stage with a raw errno and no instruction: ENOTEMPTY, Directory not empty: .runs. Measured 2026-09-21, seven consecutive runs. The removal removes nothing at all -- 528 entries before, 528 after, four runs in a row counted. The module comment above REMOVE_OPTIONS says this failure is transient, racing Spotlight or an FS event listener, and sets maxRetries 5 with retryDelay 100. Seven identical failures falsify transient for this tree. Two probes narrow it. A fresh directory created inside .runs is removed by the same rmSync call with the same options, so the filesystem permits recursive removal there. And rmSync on .runs itself throws with e.path equal to .runs, the parent, not a child, after removing nothing. Nothing in the tree is a socket, fifo, symlink or carries uchg or schg. Every remaining path exists at the destination, which is a superset: 82 files against 98, 41 against 61, 190 against 204, 86 against 99, 57 against 839. So the data is safe to remove and something specific to this tree defeats the walk. What R7 asked for was that migrate completes or names what would let it complete. The verification stage now does exactly that, proven by my following it. The removal stage does neither: it repeats a raw errno that names no action, and the operator is left where they started, with 13 MB in the repository and both trees live. This is the same defect one stage further along, and it is the honest follow-up rather than something phase 4 failed to do -- the packet named the copy step, and the copy step is fixed.

The repository largest suite cannot be both safe and declarable, and now there are numbers on both sides. Measured 2026-09-22 on this machine. node --test test/engine/ with the parallel default: 158 seconds, and killed twice with no exit code at 91 percent swap, which exhausted a node whose work was sound. The same command with --test-concurrency=1, run once memory had freed to 4.1 GB of swap: 1035 seconds, 368 tests, 368 passing. VERIFICATION_LIMITS.maxTimeoutSec is 600. So the parallel form fits the cap and is not safe under load, and the serial form is safe and exceeds the cap by 72 percent. There is no setting of that one command where both hold. I have been leaving test/engine/ out of verification arrays since phase 3 on the grounds that I could not measure it -- the attempt was killed for low memory. That instinct was right and the reason was wrong: the real reason is that the honest measurement does not fit. Three candidate resolutions, none of which belongs in a phase already authored. Split the directory into declarable groups and measure each, which is bookkeeping the author must redo whenever the suite grows. Raise maxTimeoutSec, which weakens a bound that exists so a packet cannot hang a run. Or let a verification entry declare its own concurrency and have preflight --time-verification measure it under that flag, so the number the author declares is the number the runner will see. The third is the only one that makes the author measure what will actually run, which is the rule this repository already states. Recording as the campaign closes rather than acting: every phase of this campaign has had to work around this, and the workaround -- name specific files instead of the directory -- is what phases 3, 4 and 5 all did.

Brought by Ford from frb-linux, reproduced on this Mac with timestamps, and confirmed in the code here. A run that fails before any node runs never becomes terminal, and the phase stays held until the operator cancels it by hand. Fords sequence: the run died in preflight at 18:04 with codex reported no version, next began pointing at it with resume, a fresh plan aborted over it, and only a manual cancel released the phase. Three manual cancels in four planning attempts in one afternoon. The mechanism is scheduler.mjs:228. The only prior occupant a fresh launch may move aside is one carrying cancel.request.json with a stale lock; anything else throws run already exists. The comment above it states the intent plainly and the intent is right: the operators evidence is never silently claimed. The trap is that the refusal does not distinguish a run holding evidence from a run holding nothing. A controller that died in preflight left an empty nodes directory, no attempt branch, no integrated head and no candidate ref. Claiming that path claims nothing. This is not covered by 15e1e24, which made cancel preserve integrated work before releasing git names. That fix is about what cancel does when invoked; this is about a run that never reaches cancel. Two distinct paths, and I told Ford so after checking rather than assuming my own fix covered their report. Candidate shape, not a design: a launch may claim a prior run directory that demonstrably holds no evidence -- no node ever left pending, no attempt branch, no integrated head -- and must say in one line that it did and what it found there. Anything holding evidence keeps refusing exactly as today. Same family as the migrate removal finding: an operation the product could complete on its own but instead requires a gesture the operator has to know to make.

Phase 5 (R10) landed on main as e550650, one file and 531 lines, and src/engine/cancel.mjs is unchanged. That is the honest outcome the packet named: the requirement was verification, not repair, and the code held. Seven tests now drive every path I had measured as never executed -- signalling the controller, escalating SIGTERM to SIGKILL, confirming death rather than assuming it, terminating a recorded invocation, refusing while one survives, cancelling an active verification attempt -- plus phase 1s ordering under a kill that takes time. All seven green, and zero processes left behind, which the run reported and I confirmed separately. Two things the node did better than the packet asked. The escalation is logically airtight rather than merely deterministic: the fixture records each SIGTERM and survives it, so a corpse can only mean SIGKILL, which removes timing from the proof entirely. And the reaping is three finally blocks plus a process exit handler, with the reason written down -- a finally does not run when the test process itself dies hard, and this repository has collected orphan runners alive for days. My constraint asked for the finally; the node saw past it. Attempt 1 failed for a reason worth keeping rather than hiding: its fixtures wrote node state shapes the run never produces, so readRunNodes refused before cancel could start. I traced that to cancel.mjs:58 from the log while it was still running, and the workers own diagnosis matched. The cost was one revision, which is what the revision budget is for.

Ten requirements, five phases, thirteen runs, USD 1.88. The thesis held: the durable state faberun keeps must be complete, reachable, the operators alone, and repairable. Cancel no longer orphans integrated work; a suite run leaves the operator home untouched and a ratchet measures the effect rather than an import; a journal note that does not fit is refused instead of shortened; a proof whose filter selected no test is no longer a proof; an attention belongs to one campaign or none; a record written before a field existed is repaired; a migration refusal carries what would let it finish; and cancel is finally verified against a process that is genuinely alive. What this campaign actually taught is not in its requirements. Nine of its thirteen open questions were found by running it, not by planning it -- including the sharpest one, that a gate certifying nothing is indistinguishable from a gate that passes. That appeared three times in three shapes: a DoD filter matching no test, a verification killed by memory reporting as a failed test, and a pull request with no checks reported for two opposite reasons. The planner contested both plans it was given and I authored both contracts by hand. That is not a verdict against it: both times its objections were real, and once it produced a decomposition better than my instinct. But it never closed a phase on its own, and twice its revision budget was spent on malformed output rather than on substance. Four workers taught me something my packet had wrong: that appending a reporter after a test file is a silent no-op, that 26 files already scope the home in two legitimate idioms, that a CI assertion had to fold into an existing step, and that a fixture ignoring SIGTERM makes an escalation provable without timing. I was wrong in public five times and corrected each. The campaign leaves thirteen measured open questions, which is the honest inventory for whoever runs the next one.
